title: 6 Month Marathon Training Plan (Miles & Km)
excerpt: Every week of a 24-week (6 month) marathon schedule in miles and km. For new or returning runners at 10-15 mi (16-24 km) a week; peaks at 40 mi (64 km).
body:
6 Month Marathon Training Plan (Miles & Km)

This 6 month marathon training plan is 24 weeks long. It is for runners with a low starting base: new runners who can run about 3 miles (5 km), or runners coming back after a long break, who currently run 10–15 miles (16–24 km) a week. It includes every week of the schedule in miles and kilometres, a pace key, and guidance on adjusting it.

Six months gives you room to build slowly. You run four days a week for the first eight weeks, then five, peaking at 40 miles (64 km) with a 20-mile (32 km) long run in week 21. Not sure which plan? Compare them here.

Who this plan is for

  • Your race is about six months (24 weeks) away.
  • You currently run 10–15 miles (16–24 km) a week, over three or four runs.
  • Your longest recent run is 3–4 miles (5–6 km).
  • You are new to the marathon, or returning after a long layoff or an injury that has fully healed.

Already running 20+ miles a week? A shorter plan will get you there with less waiting: try the 20 week plan. Training for a first marathon with 18 weeks to go? Use the beginner plan.

The full 24-week schedule (miles & km)

In weeks 1–8 you run on Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday, with optional cross-training on Friday. From week 9 a short Wednesday run is added. Thursday is the session day: strides at first, then hills, then threshold, interval and marathon-pace (MP) work.

Pace key

  • Easy: conversational, about 60–90 s/mi (35–55 s/km) slower than goal marathon pace.
  • Long run: easy pace, 45–90 s/mi (30–55 s/km) slower than goal marathon pace, except segments marked @ MP.
  • MP: your goal marathon pace.
  • T (threshold): comfortably hard, the pace you could race for about an hour. Roughly 25–40 s/mi (15–25 s/km) faster than MP. Jog 2 min between reps.
  • I (intervals): 5K–10K effort, roughly 50–80 s/mi (30–50 s/km) faster than MP. Jog 90 s–2 min between reps.
  • Hills: 60 s uphill at 5K effort; jog back down.
  • Strides: 20 s quick and relaxed at the end of an easy run. Walk back to recover.
  • Workout distances include a 1–2 mi (2–3 km) warm-up and cool-down.

How the 24 weeks are built

The plan works in four-week blocks: three weeks of building, then a cutback week (weeks 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20).

  • Weeks 1–8, base: easy running only, plus strides. Mileage rises from 12 to 19 miles (19 to 31 km), and the long run builds from 4 to 8 miles (6 to 13 km).
  • Weeks 9–12, strength: a fifth day is added, along with short hill repeats and your first threshold session.
  • Weeks 13–16, build: regular threshold and interval sessions. Long runs reach 14 miles (23 km).
  • Weeks 17–21, marathon-specific: MP running and long runs of 15–20 miles (24–32 km). The 20-miler in week 21 is the peak, at 40 miles (64 km) for the week.
  • Weeks 22–24, taper: three weeks of 33, 25 and 8 miles (53, 40 and 13 km) before the race.

The taper is three weeks, not longer. The extra time in a six-month plan goes into the base at the start, where it does the most good.

How to adjust the plan

  • You have more than 24 weeks: keep running weeks 5–7 at that level, with a cutback every fourth week, until 24 weeks remain. Then start at week 1. Don't stretch the peak.
  • Weeks 1–8 feel too easy: good. Resist adding mileage. If you are already above 15 miles a week, the 20 week plan is a better match.
  • Weeks 1–8 feel too hard: use run-walk intervals, or repeat a week. You have enough slack to repeat two weeks and still finish on time.
  • Kilometres: follow the km values. They are rounded.
  • Illness or injury: after a break, repeat the last full week you completed rather than jumping ahead.
  • Pain or injury: pain that changes how you run, or doesn't ease within a few days, means stop and see a doctor or physio. Don't run through it.

Fueling, strength and race week

Use the long runs from week 13 onward to practise race fueling, taking carbohydrate every 30–40 minutes. The early base phase is the best time to start strength training twice a week, because the running load is still light. Details are in our guide to what a marathon plan should include.

FAQ

Is 6 months enough to train for a marathon?

Yes. Six months is enough for most healthy adults who can already run about 3 miles (5 km). It leaves time to build a base before marathon-specific work and to repeat a week or two if you get sick. If you can't yet run 3 miles, spend 6–8 weeks building to that first.

Can I train for a marathon in 6 months with no running experience?

Some people do, but it's tight. A safer route is a few months of regular running before week 1 of this plan, or choosing a half marathon as your first goal. Check with a doctor before starting if you have a health condition.

Is there a 6 month marathon plan for intermediate runners?

If you have run marathons before and already cover 30+ miles a week, you don't need 24 weeks of marathon training. Run 6 weeks of consistent easy mileage with strides, then follow our 18-week intermediate plan. That adds up to six months, with the hard work concentrated in the right place.

How many miles a week does a 6 month marathon plan reach?

This plan peaks at 40 miles (64 km) in week 21. That is plenty to finish a first marathon well, as long as the build is gradual.
keyTakeaway: Six months is enough for most runners who can already run 3 miles: eight weeks of easy base, then gradual build blocks to a 20-mile long run and a three-week taper.
